title: Law as Code & the AI Power Shift
author: Scott Shapiro

st.t: Agentic workflows: Tacit expertise resists easy transfer
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s core view that dependable legal AI requires task-specific workflows rather than a universal chatbot, and materially extends it by mapping different legal tasks to different technical methods. It also reinforces retained human checkpoints through systematic checking of LLM-generated case claims, while treating practice-specific models as a possible way to encode accumulated expertise.

st.t: Delivery economics: AI pressures pricing and apprenticeship

st.t: Reliable delivery: Legal engineering bridges capability and service
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s emphasis on reliable, bounded deployment rather than broad claims of AI replacement, and materially extends it by proposing automated reasoning/formal methods as a distinct assurance route for law that can be translated into logic. It appropriately presents this as a conditional promise, not empirically validated performance.

st.an: Shapiro accepts the cluster’s core view that legal AI has jagged, task-specific capabilities requiring human expertise and accountability. He materially extends it by mapping distinct forms of legal reasoning to different computational methods and advocating narrow, explainable, practice-specific systems rather than general-purpose legal AI.

kp.k: AI could make increasingly complex law usable
kp.d: Shapiro presents law as a social technology enabling cooperation and coordination, whose growing complexity creates demand for supplementary technology. He frames legal AI as a possible next step in law's evolution, including democratizing legal information, but stresses that beneficial distribution depends on what people build rather than technological inevitability.
qs: So AI for law becomes like the next step in law's evolution.
The technology has to be built and has to be built for certain purposes, whether it helps people or whether it helps really rich people, you know, or bad people.

kp.k: Understanding contracts does not necessarily confer bargaining power
kp.d: Against a host's suggestion that consumer agents might negotiate terms of service, Shapiro argues that adhesion contracts, limited alternatives and users' priorities constrain meaningful change. He expects agents to explain adverse terms more readily than renegotiate them; collective agent bargaining is raised by the host, not established as an outcome.
qs: But the point about terms of service is they tend to be contracts of adhesion.
It's just going to tell me the terrible things and I'm going to click, I agree.
what's driving clicking behavior in this case is very low cost to most users and the inability to change it anyway, even if you knew what it was.

kp.k: Regulatory automation extends beyond lawyers to operational workers
kp.d: Shapiro identifies heavily regulated industries as a major application because employees, managers and call-center workers routinely apply legal rules without specialist legal training. His calculator analogy describes rule engines supporting everyday compliance decisions, such as insurance coverage and employee-benefit reimbursements, rather than exclusively automating law-firm work.
qs: They're applied by employees, managers and companies, officers and companies, people at call centers who answer questions about how to use your insurance or whether you can withdraw funds from your flexible spending account to reimburse child care.
I think now we'll be able to use sophisticated rule engine machines to determine what regulations require.

kp.k: AI may industrialize loophole discovery and contractual exploitation
kp.d: Shapiro predicts algorithmic searches for weaknesses in contracts, statutes and regulations, describing this as computational jurisprudence. He highlights private-debt covenants and recounts the transcript's 'Jscrew' example as an existing form of contractual exploitation. The host adds the possibility of searching a million contracts at scale. Shapiro expects sophisticated, wealthy actors to benefit disproportionately because formal representation, execution and monetization require expertise; these are predictions, not measured results.
qs: I could also use it to see how to avoid my legal obligations by engaging in what a hacker would say exploitation behavior.
Except for the people who are going to be able to figure out how to exploit these things are gonna be the ultra rich.
I mean, to find a loophole, you have to kind of create a formal representation of what the law is trying to do. And then you try to figure out a way to exploit it.
It's like you have computer code out there that's been around for decades and nobody's ever looked for bugs.

kp.k: Formal methods underpin Shapiro's regulatory automation product
kp.d: Describing his own company, Leibniz AI, Shapiro says it converts regulatory materials into first-order logic and uses theorem provers to derive decision trees and question workflows. Section 125 of the Internal Revenue Code and associated regulatory materials provide his example. He claims the system returns correct answers with proofs identifying the rules used; the transcript supplies no independent validation of those product claims.
qs: And so what we do is we take that and we use, and we convert that into a mathematical formalism. In our case, first order logic.
It takes the code, converts it into logic, then theorem provers show all the possible combinations of moves you can make that is creating a legal decision tree.
Exactly, so when you're finished, it tells you exactly what rules it needed and gives you a proof as to why that you got the answer that you got.

kp.k: Legal reasoning requires domain-specific methods and contestability
kp.d: Shapiro distinguishes deductive rule application from case-based reasoning involving vague standards. He considers employee benefits suitable for formal methods but rejects applying the same pipeline to constitutional law, negligence, undue influence or SEC regulation. In response to a host's challenge about determinacy, he describes 99.99% correctness as a desired standard, not an observed accuracy rate, and insists users must remain able to dispute the encoded interpretation.
qs: And that means that what the technology and the tools that we build should be appropriate to the use case, and we should not over claim.
That would be a terrible idea for SEC regs, for security regulation.
What we care about is something that gives the right answer, 99.99% of the time, but which does not choke off the possibility of dissent.
but it's always up to human beings to say, even though this is the deductive consequence of the plain meaning of the text, that's not the law.

kp.k: Case-based tools should organize information for human judgment
kp.d: Shapiro favors LLM pattern matching for inductive, case-based reasoning, coupled with checks that cited cases exist and concern what the output says. He describes interfaces that expose the underlying cases for human reading and advocates making a 'loop for the human.' Although he sometimes uses hallucination rhetorically when discussing creativity, the exchange explicitly distinguishes novel legal arguments from fabricated cases.
qs: We always check to see does the case exist? If it does exist, is it about what the response says is?
These AI tools should bring them all the information they need in order to make a determination given their client's needs.
I think LLMs are great tools, but we better have systems in place to make sure that whatever they say is checkable.
Not making up cases, but seeing new possibilities for novel argument.

kp.k: Private work product may support specialized legal models
kp.d: Shapiro speculates that frontier models' legal reasoning is constrained by their lack of access to high-quality private legal analysis. He envisages practice groups training narrow models on their own historical work, retaining them internally or renting them to other firms if privacy-preserving arrangements prevent leakage. He offers no estimate of the public/private material split when asked.
qs: One of the things that I think really holds back models like them from being great legal LLMs, is the fact that the vast majority of the highest quality legal materials are in proprietary hands.
these firms could synthesize their past work into bespoke models

if there were some privacy preserving way of ensuring that there was no data leakage, they might be able to share it on a market place where other law firms could maybe rent, lease their models for a particular purpose

kp.k: AI could redistribute the value of professional knowledge
kp.d: Host John Morley proposes that private, AI-readable information and unique personal experience become more valuable, while knowledge already incorporated into models loses scarcity value. Shapiro agrees and predicts rising value for high-quality lawyering. This is a conceptual market argument, not evidence of measured changes in lawyer compensation or firm revenues.
qs: Anyone who's sitting on a trove of private information that's legible to an AI model now has an asset that was much more valuable than it was three years ago.
What's less valuable is knowledge that's already been used to train an AI model.
the value of really good lawyering is going to get much higher because the less valuable lawyering already got used to train the AI.

kp.k: Educational feedback could become a legal training asset
kp.d: Shapiro proposes using iterative student drafts and faculty comments to train legal models, comparing this instructional process to reinforcement learning. He suggests commercial licensing could help universities replace lost federal funding while nonprofit access could serve public needs. He specifies voluntary student donation of work. These are proposed arrangements, not reported licensing programs or demonstrated training results.
qs: somebody produces an output, it's called their homework, it's called their draft brief, draft memo
This is some way that we could maybe plug up funding gaps that we're losing from the federal government by using our assignments as ways of training an AI model and then licensing it out.
I would suggest it would be donation, a purely voluntary scheme

kp.k: Clinical AI projects target unmet civil legal needs
kp.d: Shapiro reports that Yale's Legal AI Lab works on tools for low-income households and legal clinics, including benefits eligibility and an exploratory jurisdiction-specific eviction-defense tool. He expects clinic efficiency to permit more clients and pro bono services. The lab also teaches law students how to train models, reflecting his expectation that this will become part of their future work. No client-outcome or efficiency measurements are provided.
qs: One is to take this rule-based decision-making pipeline that I described earlier and trying to use it for either enabling low-income households to claim social benefits that they don't claim because the rules are so complicated, or answer their questions when they don't have access to lawyers.
can we create an eviction tool, which will explain to users in particular jurisdictions what is necessary to defend against eviction proceedings?
if we can create AI tools that increase efficiency for clinics, they will be able to handle more clients and therefore engage in more pro bono services.
we try to teach students what it would mean to train an AI model, how to do it, and what to expect from it.

kp.k: Legal AI development requires interdisciplinary research partnerships
kp.d: Shapiro distinguishes competent law-firm IT and innovation work from research requiring theoretical advances, time and resources. He is skeptical that major advances will originate wholly inside firms, while acknowledging their ability to build bespoke practice-group tools. He favors close lawyer-engineer-researcher collaboration and predicts a substantial role for law schools working with computer science and engineering schools.
qs: You have to develop theoretical insights and engage in science. And that's super hard to do outside of a research community.
It's going to have to be lawyers working directly with engineers, because engineers have no idea what lawyers need.
Lawyers don't know what engineers are able to do
if I had to bet, I would say that it should kind of come out of law schools working closely with computer science and engineering schools.

kp.k: Four application domains need different technical approaches
kp.d: Shapiro separates AI applications into business administration, legal process, legal reasoning and legal prediction. His examples include billing and client tracking; discovery, litigation support, contract negotiation and drafting; rule-based versus case-based analysis; and predicting decisions by juries, regulators or courts. The framework argues against treating all legal AI as a single chatbot or reasoning task.
qs: So the first would be what I call the business of law. So like how you track your clients, how you do your billing.
The second one would be legal process.
Then the third would be legal reasoning.
And the last thing is legal prediction. And this is predicting what a jury might do, what the SEC might do, what the Supreme Court might do.

kp.k: Document automation could improve work and institutional memory
kp.d: The speakers identify discovery and due diligence as promising applications for retrieval, text processing and classification. Morley argues that persistent firm technology could preserve case knowledge lost when associates depart. Shapiro asserts efficiency and accuracy advantages and expects improved associate satisfaction; a host additionally suggests faster development. These claims rely on professional experience and analogy rather than comparative performance data.
qs: retrieval, augmented generation, that is where you use semantic embeddings to search through enormous corpora of texts, is an incredibly promising way of getting at a document discovery
It's so much better to have a technology that sits inside your firm and masters the facts and doesn't forget them.
It's more efficient and it's more accurate.
I think this is a lot of the automation in law could really contribute to associate satisfaction.

kp.k: Automated classification could expand empirical legal research
kp.d: Morley recounts a study of governance in closed-end fund declarations of trust and certificates of incorporation that downloaded approximately 3000 documents and used Columbia undergraduate research assistants to code them. He predicts AI coding could make such research faster and more extensive. Shapiro endorses neural-network classification, but neither presents an AI replication or a measured accuracy comparison.
qs: Well, so we like downloaded like 3000 of these things and then had some Columbia University undergraduate RAs go through and code it all.
This is just going to render so much of the world legible and therefore available to study.
Classification is something that neural nets do really well.

kp.k: Legal users need advocacy and risk analysis, not answers
kp.d: Shapiro questions the usefulness of a generic 'ChatGPT for law' that simply returns ostensibly correct answers. He argues lawyers often need either advocacy for a client's position or dispassionate analysis of uncertainty and risk, and connects the latter to training on a practice group's own work. His criticism concerns product-task fit rather than rejection of LLM assistance.
qs: I'm a big user of LLMs.
Either they want an advocacy piece, okay, that argues for a certain position
or they want a very dispassionate analysis that doesn't come out on one side or the other necessarily, but kind of tells you what are the risks here, what are the problems here?
And that's why you want to train on your own work material

kp.k: Opaque superhuman reasoning could challenge legal legitimacy
kp.d: Asked whether AI might become the best legal mind through self-generated learning, Shapiro accepts the possibility without predicting it. Drawing an analogy with computational mathematics, he asks whether reasoning beyond human comprehension could still serve law's function of guiding conduct and publicly justifying decisions. The discussion also raises whether professionals may ethically act on recommendations they cannot justify to clients.
qs: And I don't know if that's the case, but I want to accept the possibility.
Law is not about getting the right answer. It's about getting the right answer in a way in which we can demonstrate to members of the community that it's the right answer.
Can it be law at that point, when the function of law is to guide human conduct?
Or is it like, I'm bound to only act in ways that I feel I can justify to you?

kp.d: Shapiro argues that benchmarking legal reasoning is difficult because correctness depends on contested accounts of law. Morley's example of 1000 appellate cases with model opinions differing from judges' opinions 30% of the time is explicitly hypothetical, illustrating that disagreement alone does not settle which answer is correct. The discussion concerns evaluation and benchmarking, not a measured hallucination rate.
qs: it's super difficult to evaluate benchmark legal LLMs, because it's really hard to benchmark legal reasoning.
And suppose that the opinions produced by the bot differed 30% of the time. Are the judges wrong or is the bot wrong?
So it's not like you can outsource this to computer science. This is a jurisprudential question.

kp.k: Regulatory caution reflects uncertainty about human responses
kp.d: Shapiro expresses wariness about regulating AI before observing more of its uses and human responses. He argues people tolerate human errors more readily than machine errors, using self-driving vehicles as an analogy. This is a behavioral claim and policy preference, not a legal analysis of particular professional rules or empirical evidence about error rates.
qs: Humans are much, much less forgiving when computers make a mistake than when humans make a mistake
I wanna wait a little longer to see how humans respond to AI, what the use cases are gonna be, because it's really hard to predict.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Scott Shapiro predicts differentiated legal-AI applications: explainable regulatory automation, accelerated exploitation of legal loopholes, human-centred assistance with case-based reasoning, bespoke models built on private expertise, and expanded legal-service capacity.
pts.d: Shapiro describes AI as a supplementary social technology for making increasingly complex law usable by lawyers and non-lawyers. He nevertheless doubts that consumer agents will materially renegotiate adhesion contracts: identifying objectionable terms does not overcome users' preferences or lack of bargaining alternatives. He says Leibniz AI converts regulatory materials into logic and uses theorem provers to generate decision trees, questionnaires and explanations. Separately, he predicts algorithmic searches for loopholes in statutes, regulations and contracts, including commercially lucrative races to exploit debt covenants. For case-based reasoning, he advocates LLM pattern matching supported by checks and source access, with humans making client-specific determinations. He distinguishes novel legal arguments from fabricated cases. In legal markets, he expects proprietary work product to constrain general frontier models and potentially support practice-specific models that firms retain or license. He argues that valuable personal expertise and high-quality lawyering will gain value, while some legal work will be replaced. He proposes using university teaching materials to train models, potentially generating licensing revenue and supporting nonprofit legal services. He predicts that lawyers will train models and favours interdisciplinary research partnerships as the source of major innovations. His four application domains are firm administration, legal process, legal reasoning and prediction of institutional decisions. He also claims AI-assisted document review can improve efficiency and accuracy, automation can increase associate satisfaction, and neural-network classification can facilitate legal research. Finally, he treats AI reasoning beyond human comprehension as a possibility raising questions about law's capacity to guide conduct, not as an established forecast.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: Shapiro supports his claims primarily with accounts of his company and Yale lab, professional experience, conceptual reasoning and an existing debt-contract exploitation example; he supplies no measured legal-AI performance or market outcomes.
pts.d: For regulatory automation, Shapiro describes Leibniz AI's actual technical approach using first-order logic, theorem provers and proof-producing workflows, illustrating it with Internal Revenue Code Section 125 and employee benefits. This is a founder's account, not an independently reported validation. For case-based tools, he describes checking whether cited cases exist and concern the propositions attributed to them, and enabling users to inspect the cases. For AI-enabled covenant exploitation, he cites the pre-existing J.Crew debt restructuring example, rendered as 'Jscrew' in the auto-caption transcript, and analogises underexamined debt instruments to untested software. He does not report an AI-enabled exploitation result. His private-data and university-training proposals rest on observations about privileged firm work product and iterative student drafting and teacher feedback, without a corpus-size calculation or training experiment. His views on innovation draw on meetings with firm innovation professionals and collaboration with computer-science researchers. His automation claims draw partly on his own unproductive summer-associate document review experience; no comparative accuracy, productivity or satisfaction study is given. His lab's benefits and eviction work is described as development or exploration, not demonstrated improvements in access or outcomes. He also explicitly argues that benchmarking legal reasoning is difficult because normative disagreement cannot simply be resolved by matching judicial outputs. The 99.99% figure is presented as what a tool should achieve while preserving dissent, not a measured result.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The account combines present development claims with mostly undated predictions, explicitly conditional on domain suitability, checkability, privacy protection, collaboration and socially beneficial deployment.
pts.d: In this source labelled 2026, Shapiro presents automated reasoning as possible now and describes company and lab work already underway. He predicts loophole exploitation will accelerate 'very quickly' but provides no calendar deadline. He is pessimistic about commercial frontier models doing great legal reasoning 'anytime soon' because high-quality private work product is unavailable to them. He calls the proposed market structure his guess. Formal methods are appropriate only where legal requirements can usefully be represented as precise deductive rules; he excludes constitutional standards, negligence, proximate cause, undue influence and securities regulation with vague language and interpretive dependencies. His initially categorical claim that the workflow always gives the right answer is subsequently qualified: users must be able to challenge the legal interpretation even when the deduction follows from the text. LLM use is acceptable when output is checkable, not because invented authorities are permissible. Licensing firms' bespoke models depends on preventing data leakage. University training proposals depend on voluntary student contributions and institutional stewardship; nonprofit benefits depend on actual deployment. Eviction assistance remains exploratory, and increased clinic capacity is conditional on achieving efficiency gains. He does not adopt the host's suggested timeline for an AI becoming the best legal mind; he explicitly accepts only the possibility and examines its implications. More generally, he says beneficial democratization depends on what is built and for whom.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: Shapiro anticipates different effects for corporate rule-appliers, wealthy legal arbitrageurs, law firms, associates, students, universities, clinics and people lacking legal assistance.
pts.d: Employees, managers and call-centre staff applying complex benefit and insurance rules could obtain explainable answers without requiring tax-law expertise for every interaction. Consumers could better understand terms of service without necessarily gaining negotiating power. Shapiro expects the ultra-rich and commercially sophisticated firms to be particularly well placed to exploit legal loopholes: identifying a flaw requires formalisation, and profiting from it also requires financial knowledge and execution capacity. Creditors are potential losers from debt-covenant exploitation. Law firms and practice groups holding private work product could develop distinctive models or license access, while frontier vendors face a training-data limitation. Lawyers with valuable tacit experience may retain differentiated value, but some forms of legal work will be substituted. Practising lawyers using case-based AI remain responsible for client-specific judgment and checking underlying authorities. Associates may benefit from less tedious review; students will need to learn model training. Universities could become model developers and licensors, while lawyers, engineers and researchers would need close design partnerships. Low-income households, people seeking benefits or eviction assistance, and clinic clients are the access-to-justice beneficiaries he envisages; this is distinct from corporate compliance savings. Nonprofit access and increased clinic throughput are proposals rather than reported outcomes. Judges, professionals and the wider public would face questions of justification and legitimacy if AI reasoning exceeded human comprehension.
